title: Tulip Mania: Was It Really That Crazy?
description:
Tulip mania usually brings to mind "one bulb for a house" or "all of Holland bankrupted by flowers." This episode covers only what the records show. On February 5, 1637, at an estate auction in Alkmaar, Holland, a Viceroy bulb sold for 4,203 guilders, the most expensive bulb on the auction list; economic historians estimate that a skilled craftsman then earned about 200 to 300 guilders a year. Prices collapsed after the first week of February. On February 24, delegates of the tulip traders from several towns agreed that deals made before the end of November 1636 would be paid, while later buyers could walk away by paying 10%; on April 27, the States of Holland suspended all contracts. The list of what one flower could buy, "four fat oxen, eight fat pigs...", was a comparison worked out in a verse pamphlet mocking the traders; in 1672 Abraham Munting wrote that someone bought these goods with one Viceroy, in the 18th century Johann Beckmann made it "agreed to deliver," and in 1841 Charles Mackay made it "delivered." In 1989 economist Peter Garber recalculated the prices and found most of them not clearly mad; in 2007 historian Anne Goldgar identified about 350 participants, mostly merchants and craftsmen, and found no wave of bankruptcies.

Limits: the auction list totals 68,533 guilders; the 90,000 figure includes bulbs sold privately before the auction. One 17th-century record does show a house traded for a lot of bulbs, both parties anonymous, not one bulb for one house. The sailor story has no known source, and Beckmann places it after the mania. Father Cats's letter and Goldgar's words come from the publisher's excerpt and a history.com interview. Sources are listed in the references below.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated. Historical figures are drawn as unnamed cartoon characters, not likenesses; modern researchers are not drawn.

Information as of 2026-10-20

tm101.text: February 5, 1637. Alkmaar, Holland. An auction begins.

tm102.text: On sale: tulips left by the late Winckel, the money for his children.

tm103.text: One bulb, called the Viceroy, is bid up to 4,203 guilders.

tm104.text: Economic historians reckon a skilled craftsman made 200 to 300 guilders a year.

tm106.text: The year before, a botanist sold bulbs at an agreed 7,000 guilders;

tm107.text: a pamphlet mocking tulip traders drew up a shopping list for one flower;

tm108.text: in an 1841 London book, a sailor ate something with his herring;

tm109.text: and a historian dug through Dutch archives for people ruined by tulips.

tm110.text: Paying that much for a single bulb: had the Dutch really gone mad?

tm201.text: The auction list gives the Viceroy's weight at planting:

tm202.text: 658 azen; one aas is about a twentieth of a gram.

tm204.text: The priciest tulips then bloomed in stripes.

tm205.text: Those stripes were the work of a virus;

tm206.text: it weakened bulbs; offsets came slowly,

tm208.text: The catch: it was still in the ground; from September to June, bulbs stay buried.

tm209.text: So buyers got only a contract, with delivery when bulbs were dug up in June.

tm211.text: traders met in taverns, in groups called "colleges."

tm212.text: Rules: per guilder traded, the buyer gave the seller half a stiver of "wine money," 3 guilders max.

tm213.text: How did outsiders see this craze?

tm214.text: The very day of that auction, a Haarlem priest wrote to his nephew:

tm215.text: like the plague, he said, a new disease had appeared: tulip traders' disease.

tm216.text: That June, did they get their bulbs?

tm301.text: No. After the first week of February 1637, prices collapsed:

tm302.text: most buyers refused to pay, leaving sellers holding the bulbs.

tm303.text: So did those contracts still count?

tm304.text: On February 24, delegates from many towns met in Amsterdam and agreed:

tm306.text: for later ones, the buyer may pay the seller 10% and walk away.

tm307.text: The accord also said this was to keep some, especially newcomers, from total ruin.

tm308.text: Yet Amsterdam's own traders refused to sign on.

tm310.text: On April 27, the States of Holland issued a decree: all tulip contracts suspended;

tm311.text: sellers could sell bulbs at market price now, settling with buyers later.

tm312.text: Courts mostly wouldn't hear such cases.

tm313.text: So how was the gap settled?

tm314.text: Haarlem later ruled: buyers could cancel by paying 3.5% of the contract price.

tm315.text: And that botanist from the start: did he get paid?

tm316.text: He'd told his buyer: if prices fell within six months, pay just 10%.

tm317.text: So he got 700 guilders for free and kept the bulbs;

tm318.text: his son wrote he'd rather have delivered them.

tm319.text: What was the crash written up as?

tm401.text: As a joke. That same year, a Haarlem printer put out three dialogue pamphlets mocking tulip traders.

tm402.text: The pamphlets invent two characters: Truemouth and Greedygoods.

tm403.text: Greedygoods: as my wife sees it, once rich we buy the town's best house and live on interest.

tm404.text: Truemouth replies: aren't those castles in the air a bit too big?

tm405.text: The opening's shopping list closes another verse pamphlet mocking traders:

tm406.text: 4 fat oxen, 8 fat pigs, 12 fat sheep, 1,000 pounds of cheese,

tm407.text: even a bed and a silver cup, for a total of 2,500 guilders.

tm408.text: But what it says is: in 1636, the price of one flower "could buy" all that.

tm409.text: Add a 500-guilder ship to carry it: 3,000.

tm410.text: And the traders add: that sum won't buy the best bulb.

tm411.text: How did a "could buy" comparison become a real deal?

tm412.text: In 1672, the botanist's son, Munting, published a plant book too;

tm413.text: but in the year of the mania, he was about ten.

tm414.text: He wrote that nobles, farmers, boatmen, even chimney sweeps and maids traded tulips.

tm415.text: He copied that list too, changing it to: back then, someone bought these goods with one Viceroy.

tm416.text: The flower got a name; the ship, he dropped.

tm417.text: Legend says a tulip cost as much as a house.

tm418.text: Did anyone really trade a house for bulbs?

tm419.text: Munting's book does record one: a house valued at 4,400 guilders

tm420.text: swapped for bulbs of equal value;

tm421.text: both parties are named only "so-and-so," with no date and no town.

tm422.text: In the 1700s, the German Beckmann wrote on inventions, mainly copying Munting;

tm423.text: in his hands, the list became "agreed to deliver."

tm425.text: Its first half, deals to be paid, became "void" under his pen.

tm426.text: That herring sailor first appears in his book too:

tm427.text: he took a few bulbs for onions and ate them with herring;

tm428.text: yet Beckmann places it after the mania, in a later "lesser mania."

tm429.text: That 1841 London book was by Mackay, and his main source was Beckmann.

tm430.text: In his hands, the list became "delivered"; the "void" half, he copied too.

tm431.text: The sailor's meal became a Semper Augustus worth 3,000 guilders, plus months in prison.

tm432.text: He also printed prices by weight, dated 1635;

tm434.text: Mostly they're from the crash month; the 1635 was his own addition.

tm435.text: Munting wrote: had this fools' trade lasted longer, it would have ruined all of Holland's trade.

tm436.text: By Mackay, it became: Dutch commerce was badly hit and took years to recover.

tm437.text: Did anyone later check what Mackay wrote?

tm501.text: Yes. In 1989, economist Garber recalculated with the prices that survive.

tm502.text: Most of his price records stop at February 5: the day of that auction.

tm503.text: His conclusion: most of it doesn't count as obvious madness.

tm504.text: Rare bulbs that start high then drop fast are normal in the trade;

tm505.text: only in the final month did common bulbs boom and bust, maybe a bubble.

tm506.text: And Munting's chimney sweeps and maids?

tm507.text: Remember the historian in the archives? Her name is Goldgar; her book came out in 2007;

tm509.text: a figure she says must be low, since she didn't search every town;

tm510.text: mostly merchants and craftsmen: cloth dealers most, plus some bakers, brewers and innkeepers.

tm512.text: She found no wave of bankruptcies;

tm513.text: she says the big losers were rich; 1,000 guilders lost was no disaster.

tm515.text: In her words: from what she saw, there was no real economic effect.

tm516.text: But, she says, it hurt reputations and relationships;

tm517.text: maybe not a financial crisis, but a social and cultural one.

tm518.text: So why do we love this story so much?

tm519.text: Goldgar's answer: it makes people look stupid.

tm520.text: Remember that opening auction? Its price list and those jokes have been bound in one volume since 1643. File closed.

tm521.text: First heard of tulip mania in a textbook, an investing book, or online?

tm522.text: Only what the records show, here. Subscribe to open files with us.
